text:
A patient may need a tracheostomy when the upper airway is blocked or when breathing support and secretion clearance will be needed for a long time, so air can reach the lungs through an opening in the neck instead of a tube through the mouth or nose. Common reasons include trauma, tumors, swelling, neurological illness, difficulty weaning from a ventilator, and bilateral vocal-cord paralysis that obstructs the airway. A tracheostomy tube sits in the trachea below the larynx and bypasses the vocal cords; it does not restore cord movement or directly treat paralysis.

CONFIDENCE: 92
